# OpenAI dumps 722 proofs on mathematics

On 6 October 2026, OpenAI posted **722 AI-written mathematics manuscripts, grouped into 372 "result families" across 17 fields**, to a public GitHub repository under an Apache-2.0 license. The papers came from an **unnamed, unreleased internal model** that was posed about 4,000 open problems, and OpenAI says the average result used about **three hours of ChatGPT Pro-equivalent thinking**. The claims include an unconditional zero-free half-plane Re(s) > 7/8 for every Dirichlet L-function (a "quasi-Riemann hypothesis"), the Mahler volume-product conjectures in every dimension, a counterexample to Kaplansky's zero-divisor conjecture, and the isomorphism of the free group factors. Any one of these would be a career-defining result, and dozens more famous problems sit behind them. Credibility is uneven, and it can be stated precisely. The strongest evidence is machine-checked Lean proofs: **162 papers have a formalized main result** and 235 families have some Lean coverage. Several of the biggest headline statements rest on clean, standard library definitions, so a fake success is hard to hide. Against that, the catalogue marks its own formal statements "unchecked", several formal statements are narrower than the headline wording, and about 137 families have no formal check at all. Reactions are only about **24 hours old**. As of 7 October no named expert has confirmed or refuted any individual theorem, and every on-record reaction concerns process (pace, credit, secrecy), not correctness. So: as a demonstration that AI can produce research mathematics at scale, this is as big as it looks, and it is the expected next step in a curve that has steepened sharply since May 2026. As a set of settled theorems, it is not yet anything. The August precedent suggests vetting ten results takes months, and vetting 722 will take years.

*Tag legend, kept from the research notes: **[V]** = primary source or full page read; **[V-repo]** = read or counted directly from the `openai/math` repository files; **[S]** = search snippet or secondary aggregator only; **[M]** = background from memory, not re-checked. Where the repository and an aggregator disagree, this report follows the repository.*

## A GitHub repo, not a journal: what actually shipped

The blog post is short. It gives none of the headline numbers. It says OpenAI is "releasing a broad range of new mathematical results produced by an internal frontier model" with "formalizations of many of the proofs in Lean", and promises reasoning summaries, compute estimates and statistics on attempted problems [V] ([OpenAI blog](https://openai.com/index/sharing-ai-progress-in-mathematics/)). The numbers come from the repository. Its README states that "the current catalogue contains **722 manuscripts organized into 372 families**". A family groups a principal result with companions, consequences or alternative proofs [V-repo] ([openai/math](https://github.com/openai/math)). The `preprints/` folder has exactly 722 subdirectories, each with PDF, LaTeX and a BibTeX entry whose sole author is "OpenAI". The repo is a single "Initial commit" (14:58 PDT, 6 Oct), about 3.1 GB, and the Lean library holds roughly **121,700 files and 25.9 million lines** [V-repo]. The 17 fields are the overview's subject sections. The largest by manuscript count are probability and statistical mechanics (105), algebraic and complex geometry (89) and theoretical computer science (73) [V-repo] ([overview](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/overview.pdf)). The press counts mostly agree. Scientific American, Quartz and The Decoder say 372 families, while Gizmodo's headline says **377**, citing the NYT. The repository count is 372 [V] ([Gizmodo](https://gizmodo.com/openai-dumps-377-new-math-results-on-github-publishes-hand-wringing-blog-post-2000822613); [Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/openai-unleashes-hundreds-more-math-results-upon-a-field-already-in-shock/)).

The widely quoted "162 Lean-formalized results" needs a correction. In the repo, 162 is the number of **papers** listed in `lean/formalization.yaml` as having a formalized main result. Those papers cover **185 formalized declarations**. Separately, **235 of 372 families** link to a Lean "scope" page that may cover only selected statements, and there are 405 Comparator challenge configs [V-repo] ([formalization.yaml](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/lean/formalization.yaml); [CONTENTS.md](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/CONTENTS.md)). A third-party analysis reproduces the 235/162 split [V] ([tech-insider](https://tech-insider.org/openai-722-math-manuscripts-unreleased-model-2026/)). The same catalogue describes its own status as **"Partial progress."**, its review status as **"unchecked"**, and its formalization method as "agent". So the formal proofs were themselves produced by AI, and no human has signed off that the formal statements match the papers [V-repo]. The research notes' text search found no `sorry` placeholders. Nobody on the research team built the library.

The process disclosure is thin but specific. The README says the results came from model evaluation: "We expanded these evaluations after performance on our existing mathematical evaluations saturated". The model "was posed **approximately 4,000 problems**", and output was aggregated into families "requiring an appropriate level of significance" [V-repo] ([README](https://github.com/openai/math)). Dividing 372 families by 4,000 problems gives a **~9% keep rate**, and some coverage quotes it [V] ([progressiverobot](https://www.progressiverobot.com/2026/10/07/openai-math-results-hundreds-more-major-problems/)). It is a crude ratio, since families are not problems, and OpenAI published no success rate, failure log, problem list or prompts. Two efforts broke the fixed procedure: the **Riemann-zeta zero-free-region work** and the **Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties**. The Re(s) > 11/12 zeta write-up was also "human edited for readability" [V-repo]. A spokesperson told Scientific American that almost every result came from "a single prompt handed to a single AI agent", while "some results might have taken multiple attempts". The spokesperson also said many results "are not yet understood by its own mathematicians" [V] ([Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/openai-unleashes-hundreds-more-math-results-upon-a-field-already-in-shock/)). The model is linked to OpenAI's September Navier–Stokes post, which describes "an internal model that is significantly more capable than GPT-6 Astra", trained by large-scale reinforcement learning since 28 August, "training ... ongoing" [V] ([OpenAI Navier–Stokes post](https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/)).

OpenAI's caveats are brief. The results are "at different stages of verification", "some of the unformalized results could have issues", and corrections will be versioned with old versions kept [V-repo] ([README](https://github.com/openai/math)). There is no named human reviewer, no error rate, and no journal plan. OpenAI says it consulted the IAS-hosted Advisory Group on Mathematics and AI (AGMAI) and is "exploring other community-hosted alternatives" [V] ([OpenAI blog](https://openai.com/index/sharing-ai-progress-in-mathematics/)). It rejected AGMAI's central request: on 29 September AGMAI had asked labs to **"stop testing advanced mathematical problems on proprietary models"** [V] ([AGMAI](https://agmai.org/general-sep29/)), and OpenAI says it will keep doing exactly that. A spokesperson said the company is "not bound by these recommendations" [V] ([Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/openai-unleashes-hundreds-more-math-results-upon-a-field-already-in-shock/); [Quartz](https://qz.com/openai-math-results-github-millennium-prize-100726)).

## Four headline claims, explained and stress-tested

A non-mathematician needs one idea to read this section. Lean is a proof assistant. A passing **Comparator** check means a computer has confirmed that a specific formal statement follows from Lean's kernel plus three standard axioms, with no gaps and no extra assumptions. The check does *not* show that the formal statement says what the English headline says, that the definitions are right, or that the result is new [V-repo] ([Comparator README](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/lean/ComparatorChallenges/README.md)). The practical question for each claim is how much of the formal statement rests on Mathlib, the large community-vetted library, and how much on definitions OpenAI's agents wrote themselves. The more of it is home-made, the more room there is for a subtly wrong definition that makes the theorem easy, or empty.

| Family | Claim (repo wording, paraphrased) | Lean status [V-repo] | Statement-fidelity risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| 003 | Every Dirichlet L-function, incl. ζ, zero-free for Re(s) > 7/8 | Formalized | Lowest: pure Mathlib definitions |
| 196 | Torsion-free group with zero divisors in 𝔽₂[G] | Formalized | Low: Mathlib plus a transparent local "torsion-free" |
| 087 | Mahler conjectures (symmetric and general), all dimensions | Both bounds formalized; functional versions not | Low: one local, standard polar definition |
| 197 | Torsion-free non-sofic counterexample to direct finiteness | Counterexample formalized, **but with torsion**; non-sofic not formalized | Gap between headline and formal claim |
| 287 | L(F₂) ≅ L(F₃); all free group factors isomorphic | Formalized | Highest: ~200 lines of bespoke operator-algebra definitions |
| 032 | Rational Hodge conjecture for all CM abelian varieties | **None** | No machine guarantee; also a procedural exception |

### The "quasi-Riemann hypothesis": a fixed fence around the primes' noise

The Riemann zeta function encodes the primes. The positions of its zeros control how far the actual count of primes up to x strays from its smooth average. The Riemann hypothesis says all the relevant zeros lie on the line Re(s) = 1/2. That would make the error as small as possible, about √x. What mathematicians can actually prove is much weaker [M]. Since the 1890s (de la Vallée Poussin, later sharpened by Vinogradov–Korobov in 1958) they have known only a thin zero-free sliver that hugs the line Re(s) = 1 and gets thinner as you go up. Nobody had ever proved that *any* fixed vertical strip Re(s) > θ with θ < 1 is free of zeros, even for zeta alone. Dirichlet L-functions are the analogous functions for primes in arithmetic progressions (primes ending in 7, say). For them there is an extra nuisance: a hypothetical "Siegel zero" sitting very close to 1, which has haunted the field for nearly a century.

Family 003 claims that **every Dirichlet L-function, including zeta, has no zeros with Re(s) > 7/8, uniformly over all moduli and characters** [V-repo] ([CONTENTS.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/math/main/CONTENTS.md)). For zeta that would cap the prime-counting error near x⁷/8. That is far from Riemann's √x, but it is a qualitative break with 130 years of progress [M]. The uniformity would also rule out Siegel zeros. The formal statement is the cleanest in the release. `LFunction_ne_zero_of_seven_eighths_lt_re` uses Mathlib's own `DirichletCharacter.LFunction`, has no hypotheses beyond Re(s) > 7/8 and excluding the pole at s=1, and permits only the three standard axioms [V-repo] ([Nonvanishing.lean](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/math/main/lean/OAI/NumberTheory/DirichletL/Nonvanishing.lean); [DirichletSevenEighths.json](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/math/main/lean/ComparatorChallenges/DirichletSevenEighths.json)). A community member reported rebuilding it, with "all 2,924 modules ... compiled with no errors and no warnings", and cautioned that this was "one run on one machine" and "checks the Lean proof, not the paper" [S] ([OpenAI Developer Community](https://community.openai.com/t/first-look-at-mathematics-manuscripts-from-an-internal-frontier-model-at-openai/1403886)).

There are three caveats. First, the Comparator config has `enable_nanoda: false`, so the independent second-kernel check was switched off [V-repo]. Second, the zeta work was a disclosed exception to the automated procedure and was human-edited, so it is not a pure "one prompt, one agent" result [V-repo]. Third, there is an oddity: a companion paper in the same family proves only a much weaker Siegel-zero bound, β ≤ 1 - c/log q, even though the 7/8 result already excludes all such zeros. That is not a contradiction, but specialists will ask about it [V-repo] ([lean/docs/003.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/math/main/lean/docs/003.md)). On sources: an earlier context note found aggregators split on whether the claim covered zeta only or all Dirichlet L-functions. The repo settles it: all Dirichlet L-functions, zeta included, plus finite-order Hecke L-functions over ℚ(√-3). Alex Kontorovich (Rutgers) called it "an instant Fields Medal" if it holds up [V] ([progressiverobot](https://www.progressiverobot.com/2026/10/07/openai-math-results-hundreds-more-major-problems/)). One aggregator says this was the only part to receive "extremely rigorous human review", but no primary source confirms it [S] ([BigGo](https://finance.biggo.com/news/1d522643-5fd9-4ac5-ae86-e4a5b99edfe2)).

### Mahler's conjecture: the smallest a shape and its "reciprocal" can be together

This one translates well for a physicist. Take a convex body K and form its polar body K^°, the set of points whose dot product with every point of K is at most 1. The polar is a close cousin of the reciprocal lattice in crystallography: stretch K in one direction and K^° shrinks in that direction. The product of the two volumes, |K|·|K^°|, is unchanged by stretching. The ball is known to maximize it [M]. Mahler conjectured in 1939 that for centrally symmetric bodies the *minimum* is attained by the cube (more generally the "Hanner polytopes"), and for general bodies by the simplex. Before this release it was proved only in two dimensions and, for symmetric bodies, in three (Iriyeh–Shibata, 2020) [M]. Family 087 claims both conjectures **in every dimension, with all equality cases classified** [V-repo] ([CONTENTS.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/math/main/CONTENTS.md)). The Lean pages formalize the symmetric bound |K||K^°| ≥ 4^n/n! with equality exactly for Hanner bodies, and the general bound with equality for simplices. They explicitly leave out the "functional" Mahler inequalities [V-repo] ([lean/docs/087.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/math/main/lean/docs/087.md)). The only home-made definition is the polar, `coordinatePolar K`, which is the standard one on inspection [V-repo] ([MahlerConjecture.lean](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/math/main/lean/ComparatorChallenges/MahlerConjecture.lean)). The fidelity risk is low, comparable to 003. No convex geometer had commented publicly as of 7 October.

### Kaplansky's conjectures: two different families, often conflated

A group algebra lets you add and multiply formal combinations of group elements, here with coefficients 0 or 1 (arithmetic mod 2). If some element g has finite order, g^n = 1, then zero divisors are easy to find: (1-g)(1+g+…+g^n-1) = 1 - g^n = 0. Kaplansky conjectured around 1950 that for *torsion-free* groups, with no such elements, two nonzero combinations never multiply to zero [M]. Giles Gardam disproved the stronger "unit conjecture" in 2021 using a SAT-solver search. Because the unit conjecture implies the zero-divisor conjecture, its failure did not settle the zero-divisor case, so a zero-divisor counterexample would go further [M]. A European Research Council (ERC) project was already pursuing that goal [S] ([CORDIS 101076148](https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101076148)).

The repo has **two separate families**, and coverage mixes them up. **Family 196** ("A Torsion-Free Group Algebra with Zero Divisors") claims exactly the zero-divisor disproof: a finitely presented torsion-free group G with nonzero α, β ∈ 𝔽₂[G] and αβ = 0. Its Lean statement says just that, using Mathlib's `MonoidAlgebra (ZMod 2) G` and a transparent local definition of torsion-free [V-repo] ([TorsionFreeZeroDivisors.lean](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/math/main/lean/ComparatorChallenges/TorsionFreeZeroDivisors.lean)). This is the second-cleanest headline formalization. **Family 197** is the one the README highlights and the one with a published reasoning trace. It concerns a *different* Kaplansky conjecture, direct finiteness (ab = 1 implies ba = 1), and claims a "torsion-free nonsofic" counterexample. Its Lean page admits that the formalized construction "gives a finitely presented group with an element of odd prime order", meaning it has torsion, and that "nonsofic is outside these statements" [V-repo] ([lean/docs/197.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/math/main/lean/docs/197.md)). The formal result still refutes direct finiteness, because torsion is allowed there. But the "torsion-free" part of the headline rests only on the unformalized paper. One aggregator noticed the mismatch [S] ([kingy.ai](https://kingy.ai/blog/openai-math-722-manuscripts-results-proofs-compute-costs/)). Another lists the zero-divisor counterexample as Lean-checked without distinguishing the two families [S] ([cellcog](https://cellcog.ai/blog/openai-math-results/)).

### Free group factors: an "all or nothing" question answered "all"

Von Neumann algebras are the operator algebras behind quantum mechanics. Each discrete group produces one. The free group on n generators produces L(F_n), and whether L(F₂) and L(F₃) are the same algebra has been open since the Murray–von Neumann era. Work by Voiculescu, Dykema and Rădulescu in the 1990s showed it is all or nothing: either every free group factor is isomorphic to every other, or none are. Most experts expected "none" [M]. Family 287 claims **"all"**: L(F₂) ≅ L(F₃), all interpolated free group factors are isomorphic, and their common fundamental group is ℝ_>0 [V-repo] ([CONTENTS.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/math/main/CONTENTS.md)).

This is the clearest conflict between sources. Early aggregator reports said the result had no Lean proof [S] ([cellcog](https://cellcog.ai/blog/openai-math-results/); [interestingengineering](https://interestingengineering.com/ai-robotics/openai-largest-math-release-lean-proofs)). The repository on 7 October has a Lean scope page and a 225-line Comparator file, `InterpolatedFactors.lean` [V-repo] ([lean/docs/287.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/math/main/lean/docs/287.md); [InterpolatedFactors.lean](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/math/main/lean/ComparatorChallenges/InterpolatedFactors.lean)). The paper, however, does not appear by title in the 162-paper main-result list (unconfirmed). Either the aggregators were wrong or the repo changed, and the repo reading wins. The formalization is also the least trustworthy of the headline four. It builds the group von Neumann algebra, its trace, the ultraweak topology, corners, amplifications and a `NormalTracialEquiv` notion of isomorphism by hand rather than drawing on Mathlib. A quick read found them standard: the double-commutant construction, the trace formula, and the scaling (r-1)⁻¹/2 match the textbook compression formula. The integer cases also state L(F₂) ≅ L(F₃) directly [V-repo, plus the researcher's own reading]. A subtly weakened notion of "isomorphism", though, is exactly the kind of flaw that an operator algebraist must rule out by auditing those 225 lines. The fundamental-group conclusion is not separately formalized.

### Everything else: a long tail that base rates say cannot all survive

The catalogue keeps going: **Khot's Unique Games Conjecture** (family 102, Lean page for a 3SAT-to-unique-games reduction); **Hilbert's tenth problem over ℚ** answered negatively (004, no Lean link); **Kakeya** maximal conjecture in 3-D and the dimension conjecture in 4-D (074, no Lean link); the **rational Hodge conjecture for every CM abelian variety**, which via Milne would give the Tate conjecture for abelian varieties over finite fields (032, no Lean link, procedural exception); the **irrationality exponent of π is exactly 2** (017, Lean for the exponent but not the Flint–Hills consequence); the full BSD formula in Selmer corank 0/1; irrationality of Catalan's constant; the matrix-multiplication exponent ω ≤ 9/4; and integer multiplication in O(n(log n)¹⁻κ), which "disproves the Schönhage–Strassen n log n optimality conjecture" [V-repo] ([overview](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/overview.pdf); [CONTENTS.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/math/main/CONTENTS.md)). Other Lean-linked claims include uniform boundedness in Hilbert's 16th problem, Kadison's similarity problem, the Crouzeix conjecture and global smoothness for relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell [V-repo]. One analysis estimates about 20% of results are disproofs or counterexamples [V] ([latent.space](https://www.latent.space/p/ainews-quasi-riemann-hypothesis-openai)). One aggregator reports that some formal statements are narrower than their headlines (e.g. a "subsequential" Fourier result in family 130) and that the integer-multiplication result has no Lean proof [S] ([explainx.ai](https://explainx.ai/blog/openai-math-results-that-matter-expert-reactions-2026)). Quartz, citing the WSJ, says the release touches three Millennium Prize problems [V] ([Quartz](https://qz.com/openai-math-results-github-millennium-prize-100726)). "Touches" is generous. The zeta result is a quasi-Riemann result, not the Riemann hypothesis. Hodge is claimed only for the CM special case. The September Navier–Stokes claim was for a forced variant that the Clay Institute still lists as open [V] ([The Neuron](https://theneuron.ai/news/inside-openais-navierstokes-claim-the-proof-the-ai-effort-and-the-credit-fight/)).

No error, rediscovery or retraction had been reported for any headline result as of 7 October [S] ([tech-insider](https://tech-insider.org/openai-722-math-claims-mathematician-scrutiny-2026/)). That absence means little after one day. The October 2025 episode, in which OpenAI's claim that GPT-5 had "solved" ten Erdős problems turned out to be literature retrieval, was a *rediscovery* failure [M]. That failure mode is unlikely for problems as famous as these, whose open status is well documented. The live risks here are correctness of the unformalized papers and fidelity of the formal statements. Rediscovery remains more plausible among the ~700 lower-profile manuscripts, which nobody has yet searched against the literature.

## From cap sets to 722 papers in under three years

The release sits on a curve that bent sharply upward in mid-2026. The 2023–2025 milestones below are from memory [M] and were not re-fetched. The 2026 items are sourced.

| Date | Milestone | Source tag |
|---|---|---|
| Dec 2023 | DeepMind FunSearch finds new cap-set constructions | [M] |
| Jul 2024 | AlphaProof + AlphaGeometry 2: IMO silver, formal proofs | [M] |
| Jul 2025 | OpenAI and Gemini Deep Think: IMO gold in natural language | [M] |
| Oct 2025 | GPT-5 "ten Erdős problems" overclaim; post deleted | [M] |
| Feb 2026 | "First Proof" challenge: AI systems pass 7 of 10 unpublished research problems, amid "very convincing nonsense" | [S] ([arXiv 2602.21201](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21201v1)) |
| May 2026 | OpenAI model disproves Erdős's 1946 unit-distance conjecture; DeepMind AlphaProof Nexus solves 9 Erdős problems a day later | [V] ([SciAm](https://scientificamerican.com/article/ai-just-solved-an-80-year-old-erdos-problem-and-mathematicians-are-amazed)); [S] ([cryptobriefing](https://cryptobriefing.com/deepmind-alphaproof-nexus-erdos-problems/)) |
| 1 Aug 2026 | OpenAI "Astra": ten Lean-certified results (sphere packing, first explicit non-sofic group), ~$2,000 total tokens | [V] ([letsdatascience](https://letsdatascience.com/blog/openai-astra-ten-open-math-problems-2000-dollars)) |
| Aug–Sep 2026 | Human audit of the ten: "no confirmed substantive mathematical error in a principal result remains" | [V] ([arXiv 2608.14673](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14673)) |
| 8 Sep 2026 | OpenAI forced Navier–Stokes blow-up claim: ~10,000 agents, ~88 hours | [V] ([OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/)) |
| 11 Sep 2026 | Fields Medalists' open letter "A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics" | [V] ([SciAm](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/25-winners-of-maths-nobel-prize-decry-the-ai-invasion-of-their-discipline/)) |
| 25 Sep 2026 | Anthropic's Claude computes the nine-loop N=4 SYM amplitude, validated by Lance Dixon | [S] ([Anthropic](https://anthropic.com/research/yes-claude-can-do-nine-loops)) |
| 29 Sep 2026 | AGMAI responsible-release recommendations | [V] ([AGMAI](https://agmai.org/general-sep29/)) |
| 6 Oct 2026 | 722 manuscripts, 372 families | [V-repo] |

Two features of this timeline matter for judging the October release. First, the verified track record is real but narrow. When the unit-distance disproof appeared in May, Timothy Gowers said "no previous AI-generated proof has come close" to top-journal standard, and Daniel Litt called it "_the_ unique interesting result produced autonomously by AI so far" [V] ([Scientific American](https://scientificamerican.com/article/ai-just-solved-an-80-year-old-erdos-problem-and-mathematicians-are-amazed)). The August ten then survived an 18-review human audit with no surviving substantive error in a principal result [V] ([arXiv 2608.14673](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14673)). That raises the prior that formalized output from this pipeline is mostly right. Second, the scale-up is steep: ten results in August, OpenAI's claim of "more than 100 long-standing open problems" on 21 September [V] ([Superpower Daily, reporting WIRED](https://superpowerdaily.com/posts/openai-is-reportedly-preparing-a-github-math-release-as-researchers-demand-papers)), and 372 families two weeks later. Benchmarks ran out along the way. OpenAI reported GPT-6 Astra at 97.6% on FrontierMath Tier 4, and Epoch reportedly treats that tier as saturated [S] ([datalearner](https://www.datalearner.com/en/benchmarks/frontier-math-tier-4-v2)). Hence the README's line that the open-problem evaluations were expanded "after performance on our existing mathematical evaluations saturated."

The sources disagree on compute. OpenAI's own post says the Navier–Stokes effort sent 4.9 million messages and used about **300 billion output tokens across all problems attempted** [V] ([OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/)). The Neuron reports ~130 billion tokens and **~$22M**, while tech-insider, citing Nature, says "several million US dollars" [V] ([The Neuron](https://theneuron.ai/news/inside-openais-navierstokes-claim-the-proof-the-ai-effort-and-the-credit-fight/); [tech-insider](https://tech-insider.org/openai-722-math-claims-mathematician-scrutiny-2026/)). The October batch reports only an *average* of three Pro-hours per result, not per-result compute or prompts. AGMAI had explicitly asked for both [V] ([Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/openai-unleashes-hundreds-more-math-results-upon-a-field-already-in-shock/)). Commentators split on whether three hours is impressive: some say it "is not much", while Chollet questions whether gains generalize beyond verifiable domains [V] ([latent.space](https://www.latent.space/p/ainews-quasi-riemann-hypothesis-openai)).

## Generation is cheap; human understanding is now the bottleneck

**For mathematics,** the dominant establishment reaction is not "it's fake" but "it's harmful as done." The September open letter, from 25 Fields Medalists by Scientific American's count (27 in one search summary), argues that "the goals of the AI companies and the goals of the mathematical community are severely misaligned." The signatories' concern is that rushed announcements leave no time to isolate new methods or credit prior work [V] ([Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/25-winners-of-maths-nobel-prize-decry-the-ai-invasion-of-their-discipline/); [S] [Mind Matters](https://mindmatters.ai/2026/09/top-mathematicians-issue-letter-warning-about-a-rush-to-ai/)). Terence Tao, who co-chairs the IAS advisory group, posted hours before the release criticizing a "Math 1.0" mindset in which open problems are "harvested in an unsustainable fashion". He warned of Goodhart's law and proposed that labs compete on new *insights* rather than raw solutions [S] ([tech-insider](https://tech-insider.org/openai-722-math-claims-mathematician-scrutiny-2026/); [Mathstodon](https://mathstodon.xyz/@tao/117221032761877425)). The other camp wants everything public. Litt: "If we want to know the answers to these math questions, I see no reason why we should ask the company to keep them secret from us" [V] ([Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/openai-unleashes-hundreds-more-math-results-upon-a-field-already-in-shock/)). Kevin Buzzard had urged OpenAI to "simply dump" its theorems, writing "you cannot fool Lean" [S] ([unite.ai](https://www.unite.ai/openai-releases-722-math-manuscripts-from-an-unreleased-ai-model/)). The skeptical middle is MIT's Andrew Sutherland: "Until and unless they release the model and people can replicate their results ... treat any claims about one-shotting problems with a single agent as unverified. We should ask for receipts" [V] ([Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/openai-unleashes-hundreds-more-math-results-upon-a-field-already-in-shock/)). Bryna Kra says advice from about 40 mathematicians who met OpenAI in August, to publish explanatory papers, "was ignored" [V] ([Superpower Daily](https://superpowerdaily.com/posts/openai-is-reportedly-preparing-a-github-math-release-as-researchers-demand-papers)). A sharper quote attributed to Gowers and Hairer ("we ... demand that they stop") appears only in one aggregator [S] ([BigGo](https://finance.biggo.com/news/1d522643-5fd9-4ac5-ae86-e4a5b99edfe2)). AGMAI's verified wording is the milder "we ask them to stop" [V] ([AGMAI](https://agmai.org/general-sep29/)). The job is shifting from *proving* toward *selecting, verifying, interpreting and integrating*, and that labor is exactly what the letter says labs are free-riding on. Scientific American expects it to "take mathematicians months to parse" the release [S]. OpenAI promises to fund workshops on understanding AI-produced results, but gives no dates [V] ([OpenAI blog](https://openai.com/index/sharing-ai-progress-in-mathematics/)).

The most novel social effect is **scooping by a tool vendor**. Tristan Buckmaster (NYU) alleged that OpenAI's Navier–Stokes push drew on his private Codex sessions and that Sébastien Bubeck proposed excluding Anthropic's Levent Alpöge from a joint paper. OpenAI denied using unpublished user-specific data but could not rule out de-identified usage data [V] ([The Neuron](https://theneuron.ai/news/inside-openais-navierstokes-claim-the-proof-the-ai-effort-and-the-credit-fight/)). When the company that sells you a research assistant also competes on your research problems, Tao's worry follows: people stop sharing promising directions [V] ([36kr translation](https://eu.36kr.com/en/p/3977126046986497)). Alpöge himself, while raising conflict-of-interest concerns, called this "obviously the most significant moment in mathematical history" [V] ([latent.space](https://www.latent.space/p/ainews-quasi-riemann-hypothesis-openai)). Gary Marcus called that framing "absurd" [S] ([digg/Marcus](https://digg.com/ai/1zii0bc9)).

**For publishing and refereeing,** the release sidesteps every existing gatekeeper. GitHub has no moderation and no persistent DOIs, and its author line names only a corporation. That clashes with journal norms on author responsibility and with AGMAI's request for deposit in repositories "not ... controlled by any AI lab" [V] ([AGMAI](https://agmai.org/general-sep29/)). Since May 2026, arXiv has imposed a one-strike, one-year ban for "incontrovertible evidence of hallucinatory AI generation". The policy targets unchecked output, not AI use, and comes after fabricated citations rose roughly twelvefold since 2023 [S] ([CERN Courier](https://cerncourier.com/a/arxivs-one-strike-rule-on-ai/)). No journal, AMS, EMS or IMU policy on bulk AI-generated proofs turned up. OpenAI's versioned-corrections promise is a reasonable software-style substitute for errata. It does not replace refereeing, because Lean can certify logic but, as The Decoder puts it, "can't judge whether a result is mathematically relevant or original" [V] ([The Decoder](https://the-decoder.com/openai-dumps-372-ai-generated-math-proofs-on-github-telling-the-academic-world-to-keep-up/)). The likely practical outcome is a two-tier literature. Lean-certified statements will be trusted provisionally once someone audits the formal statement. Unformalized AI manuscripts will be treated as conjectures with suggestive sketches.

**For science more broadly,** spillover is already visible in theoretical physics: Claude's nine-loop amplitude, validated by Dixon at a cost of "one or two thousand dollars" [S] ([Anthropic](https://anthropic.com/research/yes-claude-can-do-nine-loops)), and the forced-fluid blow-up work. Several October claims are in mathematical physics, including the diluted-spin-glass Mézard–Parisi formula, Bloch's T³/2 law for the quantum Heisenberg ferromagnet, and Vlasov–Maxwell smoothness [V-repo] ([README](https://github.com/openai/math)). For cryptography, nothing claimed threatens deployed systems. RSA and elliptic-curve security rest on factoring and discrete-log hardness, not on zeta zeros, and a Unique Games proof is a *hardness* result [M; researcher inference]. The August closest-vector result explicitly "does not imply attacks on already deployed post-quantum systems" [S] ([cryptobriefing](https://cryptobriefing.com/openai-model-solves-math-problems/)). The real security implication is the capability itself. A system that produces deep new number theory on demand could eventually produce new algorithms, cryptanalytic ones included.

**For the AI race,** mathematics has become the public proof-of-capability for "automated research". Math is the cleanest domain for it, because answers are machine-checkable and cheap to verify relative to discovering them. OpenAI ties the release to its roadmap. It claimed the "automated research intern" milestone in September and is targeting an autonomous AI researcher by March 2028 [S] ([propakistani](https://propakistani.pk/2026/09/07/openai-says-it-has-built-an-automated-ai-research-intern/)). The Navier–Stokes post says the goal is "to inform the world about the pace of AI progress and what to expect from upcoming models" [V] ([OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/)). Each lab has a distinct position. OpenAI leads on volume and headline audacity. DeepMind emphasizes Lean-first systems on problems with checkable answers, an approach seen as more defensible [V] ([tech-insider](https://tech-insider.org/openai-722-math-claims-mathematician-scrutiny-2026/)). Anthropic has a smaller, externally validated physics showcase. No research-level Chinese results surfaced, only olympiad and prover-level systems such as DeepSeekMath-V2 [S] ([SCMP](https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-trends/article/3308566/deepseek-quietly-updates-open-source-model-handles-maths-proofs)). Competitors had not responded publicly to the 722 by 7 October, which one outlet called "competitor and market silence" [V] ([progressiverobot](https://www.progressiverobot.com/2026/10/07/openai-math-results-hundreds-more-major-problems/)). Some coverage places the release next to 2026 reporting that OpenAI is preparing an IPO, but no source argues the release was IPO-motivated, and that link rests on timing alone [S] ([Engadget](https://engadget.com/2178018/openai-may-go-public-as-soon-as-september)). The decisive limit is that **the model is unreleased**. Nobody outside OpenAI can reproduce a single result, measure the failure rate, or check how much curation sits between 4,000 prompts and 372 families.

## Conclusion

The release changes what the open question is. Before 6 October the question was whether AI could do research mathematics. After it, the question is whether mathematics can absorb research produced faster than humans can understand it. The best single indicator of how this ends is not the 722 count. It is a short list of formally clean claims (the 7/8 half-plane, the family-196 zero divisor, symmetric Mahler) where a correct build leaves little room for doubt. If specialists audit those formal statements over the coming weeks and find them faithful, the case for the headline results becomes very strong regardless of what happens to the long tail. The free-group-factor definitions, the torsion-free claim in family 197, and the unformalized Hodge, Kakeya and Hilbert's-tenth papers are where errors are most likely to surface. A few failures there would be expected, and would not undercut the core.

For a scientist reading from outside, there is a familiar pattern. Instruments that generate data faster than people can interpret it shift the scarce skill from measurement to judgment. Lean is to these proofs what a calibrated spectrometer is to raw signal: it guarantees the reading, not the meaning. The most consequential thing about this release is the precedent it sets: a company publishing unrefereed results from a model nobody else can run, while overriding the one rule its own advisory group asked it to follow. The rest of science should expect the same pattern once AI output in its own fields becomes as checkable as mathematics. All expert reactions cited here are about a day old, and the technical verdicts have not started.
